newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says N. Korea action will not affect aid.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says N. Korea action will not affect aid.

text.p: The United States accused North Korea on Wednesday of unusually aggressive provocation in sending soldiers across the demilitarized zone with South Korea but said it would not affect promised new food aid.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns also said the incident underscored the importance of starting four-party talks designed to bring a permanent peace on the Korean peninsula on Aug. 5 as planned.

"They crossed the line and (under the 1950-53 Korean War armistice agreement) they can't do that. It's a provocative act. This was definitely more aggressive than usual," Burns told a regular State Department news conference.
The United States announced earlier this week that it was more than doubling its food aid from $25 million to $52 million to meet North Korea's famine.
Burns said the incident "would have no effect on the aid" because it is aimed at helping children and the elderly, the "victims" of the North's Stalinist system.
Citing United Nations reports, he said the incident began when 14 North Korean soldiers crossed over the heavily armed DMZ into South Korea.
Seoul military officials said the North fired artillery shells at a Southern guard post in one of the worst border clashes in recent years.
U.S. officials, declining to officially accept that version, said it was unclear how the shooting started and they would wait to hear the results of a follow-up investigation.
Some 37,000 American troops are stationed in the South but no U.S. forces were involved in the clash, which occurred in an area of the DMZ 37 miles (60 km) east of Panmunjon.
Burns described the United States as "obviously very concerned by this incident" and said it should be addressed quickly by the military commission that oversees the armistice.

He said there have been many incidents between North and South over the years, all provoked by the North, and Washington wants to ensure that "needless incidents like the one this morning are not repeated and people's lives are not put into danger."

Burns said Washington was at a loss to know why Pyongyang may have provoked the incident but believes more firmly than ever that the long-awaited talks among North and South Korea, China and the United States open in New York as planned.
"This is a country that has to get with it, and it has to negotiate with us and South Korea and China a peace treaty and a permanent end to the Korean conflict," Burns said.
The United States has no indication that Pyongyang may back out of its commitment to attend the New York meeting, which is intended to make plans for actual negotiations, the spokesman added.
Administration officials communicated their concerns to North Korean officials on Wednesday and also had conversations with South Korea, a close U.S. ally.
